title: Higher laws
hookLine: he felt pulled both to the wild and to a higher, purer life (Walden 11)

cards: Dark in the woods by Walden. Thoreau is walking home with a string of fish when a woodchuck crosses his path, and something happens in him that he doesn't expect.
He feels, he says, a strange thrill of savage delight, and a strong urge to grab the animal and eat it raw. Not because he's hungry. Because of the wildness it stands for.
This is the same man who will spend the rest of the chapter writing about purity, restraint and a higher life. He doesn't hide the woodchuck moment. He opens with it.

teach.b: First, the confession. The chapter is called Higher Laws, and it begins not with a law but with that woodchuck. Thoreau wants you to see the wild in him before he says anything lofty.

Second, the two instincts. Right after, he says he found in himself an instinct toward a higher, or spiritual, life, and another toward a rank and savage one. Two pulls, in one person, at the same time.
He doesn't declare war on either: "I reverence them both." And a line short enough to keep: "I love the wild not less than the good." Reverence is a strong word.
He's not just putting up with the wild; he honors it. Fishing and hunting, he says, were often how boys first met the woods, and some grow up and leave the rod behind for something higher.

The wild was a doorway, not an enemy. Fourth, where the chapter goes. As it continues, Thoreau leans hard toward the higher pull: eating simply, drifting away from fishing, keeping the body clean as a kind of worship.
He ends with a farmer on his doorstep after a long day, hearing a flute, and suddenly asking himself why he lives so small when a glorious life is possible.
Readers argue about whether Thoreau kept his balance or tipped over into strictness. But he started with both pulls held up to the light, and called both worthy of reverence.

how: Readers of Higher Laws often notice that Thoreau names both a wild instinct and a spiritual one in himself, and take from him a way of honoring both rather than despising either.

games.q: you're Thoreau. you feel a wild, almost savage pull, and also a pull toward a purer, higher life. what do you write?
o: that the wild must be crushed.
that only the wild is real.
games.why: "I reverence them both." the chapter leans toward the higher life, but it starts by honoring both pulls.

practice: Find the wild in you right now, the part that wants to run, or eat, or shout, or walk out into weather, and without scolding it, name it and breathe with it.
Then find the other pull, the part that wants quiet, or clean, or good, and name that too. Let one sit on each side of you, like two companions on a bench; neither has to win today.
